extracted.intended_audience: general readers, librarians, legal researchers, and those interested in censorship/intellectual freedom
extracted.subtask_description: A concise encyclopedic summary of the California Court of Appeals decision Moore v. Younger (1976) concerning the application of California's Harmful Matter Statute to librarians and access to materials for juveniles.

rubrics_metrics.name: California Harmful Matter Statute (scope/ambiguity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision 'originated from a somewhat ambiguous law, California's Harmful Matter Statute.' The Attorney General 'claimed that individual librarians could be prosecuted for giving juveniles access to questionable reading materials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statute was the legal basis for the complaint; its ambiguous wording raised questions about the reach of criminal liability for distributing or providing access to materials deemed harmful to minors (see Penal Code Section 313-313.5). The ambiguity prompted the legal challenge by the librarian plaintiff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Librarian exemption (holding in Moore v. Younger)
rubrics_metrics.description: In February 1976, Moore won his case: 'All librarians in California were found to be exempt from the Harmful Matter Statute by the California Court of Appeals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appellate holding established that librarians could not be prosecuted under the statute for providing juveniles access to questioned reading materials, a result bearing on intellectual freedom and censorship policy in libraries.
